newsitem.title: KENYA: Rains arrive in E.Africa, brighten food prospects.
newsitem.headline: Rains arrive in E.Africa, brighten food prospects.

text.p: Rains battered most food growing areas of East Africa for the first time since December on Tuesday brightening hopes of a better 1997/98 food crop, weather and crop officials said.
Coffee growers reported showers in northern Tanzania, weather officials reported heavy rains in western Kenya while farmers spoke of torrents in Uganda's growing Soroti district.
"There have been some rains here. There have also been reports of rain in the northern Moshi area," a resident in the Tanzanian capital of Dar es Salaam told Reuters by telephone.
The Kenyan capital Nairobi was overcast with clouds but still saw no rains. But weather officials said the tea growing town of Kisii had received 10 millimetres of rain.

"Soroti town received torrential rains, much earlier than an April forecast provided by the weather department. Rains are now seen spreading across Uganda," a Ugandan coffee trader told Reuters by telephone from the capital Kampala.
Kenya and Uganda have forecast lower 1996/97 and 1997/98 coffee crops because of a severe drought in East Africa.

In Nairobi the Famine Early Warning System (FEWS) said drought monitors had predicted that the long rains would be near normal in west Kenya while the drought-hit pastoral and marginal agricultural areas would experience below-normal rainfall.

"Significantly below-normal production countrywide in both the long and short rains season in 1996 has resulted in very high maize prices," FEWS, a project of the U.S. Aid for International Development (USAID), said in a report.

The Kenyan government estimates relief and commercial import needs at 639,000 tonnes of maize and 243,000 tonnes of beans and has lifted a ban on maize imports and removed all duties and taxes on maize, pulses, milk and rice for relief distribution.
Up to 70,000 tonnes of maize imported from South America and Southern Africa are on transit to Kenya, shippers said.

FEWS said that in Uganda, the harvesting of the second-season crops was complete and production appeared to have been about 30 percent below normal because rains were either poorly distributed or excessive in critical growing periods.

But it added that the reduced production did not pose a threat to national food security because most households were able to buy food in the market and the needy could get food through international relief programmes.
FEWS said in northern Uganda, the effects of massacres and mass kidnappings by the rebel Lord's Resistance Army and the West Nile Bank Front had disrupted food production and trade.

"Many residents of Arua, Nebbi, Moyo, Gulu and Kitgum districts were unable to tend their fields during the second season or to complete harvesting of whatever crops they managed to cultivate," FEWS said.

It said that following the most recent wave of violence in the hardest hit districts of Gulu and Kitgum, the U.N. food aid agency WFP estimated that 220,000 people out of an approximated population of 849,900 were affected by the conflict.
FEWS and government agencies said it was too early to provide detailed estimates of food production for 1997/98.
